title: Matthew 7:24–29
context: The Sermon on the Mount closes with two builders—hearing-and-doing versus hearing-without-doing—then Matthew’s narrator notes the crowds’ astonishment: Jesus taught with authority, not as their scribes.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On The Sermon on the Mount closes with two builders—hearing-and-doing versus hearing-without-doing—then Matthew’s, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He taught them - The multitudes, as one having authority - With a dignity and majesty peculiar to himself as the great Lawgiver, and with the demonstration and power of the Spirit: and not as the scribes - Who only expounded the law of another; and that in a lifeless, ineffectual manner.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 7:24–29)

reformed.quote: Every one, therefore, who heareth As it is often difficult to distinguish the true professors of the Gospel from the false, Christ shows, by a beautiful comparison, where the main difference lies. He represents two houses, one of which was built without a foundation, while the other was well-founded.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 7:24–29)

verses.text: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wisdom is hearing plus doing. Jesus’ words are the rock; obedience is how one builds upon them. The invitation is universal in form—“everyone” who hears and does.

Arminian readers treasure responsible response: grace enables putting the sermon into practice. Christ’s teaching is the only sure foundation for a life that lasts.
verses.reformedNotes:
“These words of mine” claim unique authority. The wise builder is defined by obedient hearing. Rock is Christ’s word received in living faith.

Such doing comes from a heart made wise by God. The parable does not teach self-salvation; it displays discipleship that grace produces.

verses.text: The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.
verses.arminianNotes:
Storms come to both houses. Stability is not the absence of trial but foundation. The rock-built house stands because it was founded rightly—on Jesus’ words obeyed.

Persevering obedience under grace prepares you for rains, floods, and winds. The promise is endurance, not ease.
verses.reformedNotes:
Providence sends weather that tests foundations. The house stands because of the rock—cause named. Trial reveals what grace has built.

Security rests on the foundation, not on the builder’s swagger. Christ’s word upheld in faith holds when judgment-winds blow.

verses.text: Everyone who hears these words of mine and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hearing without doing is folly. Same sermon, opposite response: sand instead of rock. Exposure to truth without obedience is spiritually dangerous.

Classical Arminians press accountability: you may hear and refuse to practice. Grace invites doing; folly is a free choice against wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes:
Folly is not lack of information but refusal to obey. Sand looks workable until the storm. Mere hearers build lives that cannot last.

Common grace may give hearing; saving grace produces doing. The contrast exposes empty profession inside the crowd that listened.

verses.text: The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell—and its fall was great.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Identical storm, opposite end: collapse, and great was the fall. Jesus does not soften the tragedy of a life that heard Him and did not obey. The sermon ends with pastoral alarm meant to save.

Build on the rock now—hear and do by the grace God supplies. Shared confession: the fall of sand-built religion is catastrophic and unnecessary if one turns to obey Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fall is great because the claim was great and the foundation false. Final judgment and life’s crises alike unmask sand. Jesus loves His hearers enough to terrify them out of folly.

Only the rock holds. Assurance belongs to those founded on Christ’s words in Spirit-wrought obedience; the parable drives us to Him, not to panic self-construction.
verses.keyContrast: Both require hearing and doing Jesus’ words. Arminians commonly stress grace-enabled obedient response versus foolish refusal; Reformed readers commonly stress Spirit-produced obedience on Christ the rock, with storms revealing true foundations.

verses.text: When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching,
verses.arminianNotes:
The sermon ends; amazement begins. Crowds feel the weight of “these things”—ethics, warnings, promises, and the claim of Lordship. Astonishment is a fitting first response to hearing Jesus.

Arminians note that amazement must mature into obedient faith. Grace that arrests attention also calls for entering the narrow gate. Jesus’ teaching is not ordinary religious advice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew marks completion: Jesus finished these sayings. Crowd astonishment is historical and theological—God has spoken in His Son with unique force.

Reformed readers see providence preparing the next scenes of authority in deed. Wonder is gift; saving faith is still required beyond the crowd’s awe.

verses.text: for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason for astonishment is authority. Scribes leaned on tradition’s citations; Jesus speaks as the Lawgiver fulfilled and the Judge who will say “I never knew you.” Hearers must decide what to do with that claim.

Authority invites trust and obedience freely rendered under grace. You are summoned to build on His words, not merely to admire them. Shared confession: Jesus’ authority surpasses every secondary teacher.
verses.reformedNotes:
Authority versus scribal manner is Matthew’s key. Jesus does not merely interpret Torah; He authoritatively declares the Father’s will and His own lordship.

This is the voice of the incarnate Son. The contrast with scribes magnifies Christ alone. Crowds may marvel; the elect are brought to submit—yet the text leaves every reader under the same authoritative Word.
verses.keyContrast: Both marvel at Jesus’ unique authority over against the scribes. Arminians often stress the summons to grace-enabled obedient response to that authority; Reformed readers often stress the divine Son’s sovereign right to command and the Spirit’s work producing true submission.
